```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
```

## Abstract

Camera-trap network performance depends on battery reliability, yet battery choice and service planning are often treated heuristically. We analyzed deployment-interval battery outcomes from a Tasmanian camera network using reproducible survival workflows. The core frequentist analysis combines Kaplan-Meier summaries, a region-stratified Cox proportional hazards model with camera-cluster robust inference, and competing AFT models (Weibull, lognormal, loglogistic) trained on TAS-CAM regions. Predictions are checked only for supported battery/flash strata in the held-region South West (SW) data from the same project and protocol; this is not independent external validation. Bayesian review outputs are retained as corroborating rather than primary evidence. Output artifacts are generated by a `targets` DAG and rendered directly into this manuscript.

## Introduction

Battery failure in camera networks creates two linked costs: data loss through camera downtime and field logistics burden from servicing. Prior work and practitioner experience suggest high-quality lithium batteries can outperform cheaper alternatives, but comparative evidence under field conditions is often sparse, confounded by service schedules, and difficult to reproduce.

This project modernizes a legacy analysis into a fully reproducible pipeline and produces manuscript-ready artifacts directly from code. The phase-1 objective is to establish robust comparative modeling using:
1. Kaplan-Meier survival curves for descriptive differences.
2. Cox proportional hazards modeling for covariate associations.
3. AFT model comparison to support predictive planning.

The manuscript draft here is intentionally code-linked: all reported tables and figures are generated under `outputs/` and consumed without manual copy-paste.

### Survival Modeling

The phase-1 pipeline fits:
1. Descriptive Kaplan-Meier curves by battery brand.
2. A Cox proportional hazards model with region stratification and camera-cluster robust inference on the TAS-CAM training subset (`ct`, `se`, `nw`, `wt`).
3. AFT models (Weibull, lognormal, loglogistic) for comparison and predictive framing on the same training subset.
4. A support-limited held-region check against the SW subset (`sw`) using horizon-specific observed vs predicted survival summaries for strata represented in training.
5. A separate testbench (`tb`) descriptive analysis that is not used in primary field-model fitting.
6. Optional Bayesian AFT model fitting using `brms` + `cmdstanr`, controlled by pipeline config and interpreted only as corroborating evidence.

Current covariate specification:
1. Battery brand (`bb`), flash type (`ft`), season (`seas`).
2. Flash-photo rate (`log_fi_pd`) and daylight-photo rate (`log_day_pd`).
3. Region handled as strata in Cox; AFT is fitted without region to stabilize predictive service-interval calculations across pooled conditions.

### SW Held-Region Check

The SW check is reported for brand/flash strata that are supported by TAS-CAM training data (see `supported_rows` versus `total_rows` in the summary table). SW-only brands are retained in descriptive reporting but treated as out-of-support for model-based prediction. Because SW belongs to the same project and protocol and has limited overlap with the training strata, this check does not establish universal transferability or independent external validation. In the summary table, `mean_observed` averages over all observed SW strata, whereas `mean_predicted`, `mae`, and `rmse` average over strata with finite predictions only, so unsupported strata can leave `mean_observed` nonzero even when the error metrics are zero.

```{r}
val_sum_path <- "../outputs/tables/validation_survival_summary.csv"
val_detail_path <- "../outputs/tables/validation_survival_detail.csv"
val_fig <- "../outputs/figures/validation_observed_vs_predicted.png"

if (file.exists(val_sum_path)) {
  val_sum <- read_csv(val_sum_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  kable(val_sum, digits = 3, caption = "Support-limited SW held-region summary by horizon (observed vs AFT-predicted survival; observed means use all SW strata, prediction/error columns use finite-prediction strata only).")
}

if (file.exists(val_detail_path)) {
  val_detail <- read_csv(val_detail_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  kable(head(val_detail, 20), digits = 3, caption = "SW held-region detail rows (first 20).")
}

if (file.exists(val_fig)) {

      status = fit_status,
      looic = looic,
      rhat = rhat_max,
      ess_bulk = bulk_ess_min,
      divergences = divergences,
      bfmi = bfmi_min,
      elapsed_s = elapsed_seconds
    )
  kable(bayes_cmp_display, digits = 3, caption = "Bayesian model diagnostics/comparison summary.")
}

if (file.exists(bayes_gate_path)) {
  bayes_gate <- read_csv(bayes_gate_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  bayes_gate_display <- bayes_gate %>%
    transmute(
      family = model_family,
      status = fit_status,
      gate = gate_status,
      rhat = rhat_max,
      ess_bulk = bulk_ess_min,
      divergences = divergences,
      fail_reasons = fail_reasons
    )
  kable(bayes_gate_display, digits = 3, caption = "Bayesian strict-gate diagnostics status by model family.")
}

if (file.exists(bayes_coef_path)) {
  bayes_coef <- read_csv(bayes_coef_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  if (nrow(bayes_coef) > 0) {
    bayes_coef_display <- bayes_coef %>%
      transmute(
        family = model_family,
        term = term,
        estimate = estimate,
        q2.5 = q2.5,
        q97.5 = q97.5,
        time_ratio = time_ratio
      )
    kable(head(bayes_coef_display, 20), digits = 3, caption = "Bayesian coefficient summary (first 20 rows).")
  } else {
    cat("Bayesian coefficient table omitted in this run.")
  }
}

if (file.exists(bayes_fig)) {
  knitr::include_graphics(bayes_fig)
}
```

## Service-Interval Economics

The economics layer evaluates service-interval tradeoffs using the best AFT model from the phase-1 model comparison. For each battery brand and flash type profile, we compute:
1. Expected active camera-days within service interval `T`: `E[min(X, T)]`
2. Expected downtime: `T - E[min(X, T)]`
3. Cost per active day: `(C_s + C_b) / E[min(X, T)]`

where \(C_s\) is scenario-specific service cost and \(C_b\) is battery-set cost. These are decision scenarios, not fixed universal prices. A cycle assumes a scheduled visit and replacement battery set, with no intervening rescue visit or restart after failure.

Write \(A(T)=\int_0^T S(t)\,dt\) and \(K=C_s+C_b>0\). Then the cost derivative is \(-KS(T)/A(T)^2\leq0\): extending the interval cannot increase this cost metric. Expected downtime fraction, \(1-A(T)/T\), is non-decreasing. The curves therefore describe a cost--downtime trade-off; they do not identify an unconstrained optimal service interval. Changing service cost rescales a profile's cost curve without changing this conclusion.

A manager could specify an acceptable downtime fraction or probability of failure before service, then compare costs within that constraint. No universal tolerance or monetary value of lost observations is assigned here. The evaluated intervals are 30, 37, ..., 359 days. Survival is reconstructed by quantile interpolation with a truncated tail; resulting flat cost tails must not be treated as preferred service intervals. Modelled active days and downtime also inherit the uncertainty of the last-image endpoint and the realised workload profiles. See `docs/servicing_cost_interpretation.md` for the derivation and scope.

```{r}
fig_cost <- "../outputs/figures/cost_per_active_day_vs_interval.png"
fig_down <- "../outputs/figures/downtime_fraction_vs_interval.png"

if (file.exists(fig_cost)) {
  knitr::include_graphics(fig_cost)
}
if (file.exists(fig_down)) {
  knitr::include_graphics(fig_down)
}
```

## Discussion

The Weibull AFT model is clearly preferred among the three comparable AFT distributions and supplies conditional survival and cost--downtime scenarios. The Cox model remains a separate association analysis; its global proportional-hazards diagnostic indicates non-proportionality, so coefficient estimates require qualified interpretation rather than use as the prediction engine. SW provides a support-limited held-region check within the same project and protocol, with material prediction error at intermediate horizons. The servicing curves require a management constraint before an interval can be chosen. Bayesian results remain corroborating evidence rather than a prerequisite for the primary argument.

The remaining work is manuscript production rather than a new analytical phase:
1. Synthesize the reviewed literature and populate publication-ready citations.
2. Draft the Results and Discussion around the fixed frequentist, SW, Bayesian-corroboration, and economics evidence hierarchy.
3. Finalize author metadata and journal style; the Makedoc backbone build is a private drafting proof.
